passage_text: Researchers investigated the effect of two novel cognitive training programs on reaction time in healthy adults. A total of 180 participants (age 20‑35) were randomly assigned to one of three groups: a control group (no training), Treatment A (visual‑spatial training), or Treatment B (verbal‑linguistic training). After a 4‑week intervention, participants completed a computerized reaction‑time task. The table below summarizes the mean reaction times (in milliseconds), standard deviations, and sample sizes for each group. The results suggest that both training programs reduced reaction time compared to the control, with Treatment B showing the greatest improvement.
stem: According to the table, which group had the lowest mean reaction time after the intervention?

options.D: Treatment A and Treatment B were tied

explanation: Correct: Treatment B had 440 ms, lower than 470 and 520 ms. Why the others are wrong: A) 520 ms was the highest. B) 470 ms was higher than Treatment B. D) The means were 470 and 440 ms.
trap: Thinking a larger number means better performance and choosing the 520 ms control group, when the lowest reaction time is the smallest value, 440 ms for Treatment B.

stem: Which study design best controls for confounding variables in this experiment?
explanation: Randomization of participants into three groups ensures that confounding variables are evenly distributed across groups, making the randomized controlled trial the gold standard for controlling confounders.
trap: Students sometimes think an observational study can control for confounding, but without randomization it cannot.

stem: Which design feature is most likely to introduce performance bias (differences in effort or motivation between groups)?

options.A: The control group received no activity, so participants knew whether they were being trained
options.B: The three groups had equal sample sizes
options.C: Participants were randomly assigned to groups
options.D: All groups completed the same computerized reaction-time task

explanation: Correct: participants in a no-training control cannot be unaware of their assignment, which may alter effort on the test. Why the others are wrong: B) Equal group sizes do not produce bias. C) Random assignment reduces bias. D) A common outcome task reduces measurement differences.
trap: Picking random assignment or equal group sizes as the source of bias, when the bias arises because untrained controls know they received nothing and may try less hard.

stem: Which statement is supported by the table?

options.A: The mean reaction time of Treatment B was 80 ms lower than that of Control.
options.B: Treatment A had a lower mean reaction time than Treatment B.
options.C: The Control group had the smallest standard deviation.
options.D: Treatment A and Treatment B means differed by 60 ms.

explanation: Correct: 520 - 440 = 80 ms. Why the others are wrong: B) 470 ms is higher than 440 ms. C) Control had the largest SD (45). D) 470 - 440 = 30 ms.
trap: Mixing up the direction or size of the differences, such as reading 470 versus 440 ms as a 60 ms gap or treating Treatment A as faster than Treatment B.
